facts.text: On this date in 1825, the world's first public steam railway opened in England — the Stockton and Darlington line. It ran at 15 mph, and locals assumed the speed would suffocate passengers.
On this date in 1938, Hitler, Mussolini, Chamberlain, and Daladier signed the Munich Agreement, handing Czechoslovakia's Sudetenland to Germany without a single Czech official in the room.
The Philippines contains more than 7,600 islands, yet over half the country's population lives on just 11 of them. The remaining thousands are largely uninhabited.
Tokyo's greater metro area holds 37 million people — more than the entire population of Canada — yet its violent crime rate is lower than Zurich's.
Niger has the world's highest fertility rate at roughly 6.9 births per woman. Its population is projected to surpass the United States by the end of this century.

On this date in 1998, Long-Term Capital Management's $3.6B bailout closed — a hedge fund run by two Nobel laureates that nearly collapsed the global financial system by betting on convergence trades that refused to converge.

On this date in 1907, a banking panic froze credit across the U.S., ultimately forcing J.P. Morgan to personally lock rival bankers in his library until they agreed to pool capital and stop the collapse.
The S&P 500 has closed higher on the day after Thanksgiving more than 80% of the time since 1950 — not because of shopping optimism, but because trading volume collapses and sellers simply stay home.

Berkshire Hathaway was originally a failing textile mill. Warren Buffett later admitted buying it was his worst investment decision — the sentimental purchase cost him an estimated $200 billion in compounded opportunity.

The Dutch East India Company, history's first publicly traded corporation, was so profitable at its peak that its inflation-adjusted market cap exceeds every company alive today, including Apple and Saudi Aramco.
On this date in 1905, Einstein submitted his paper on E=mc². The equation didn't appear in that paper — it arrived in a quiet follow-up three months later.
On this date in 1998, Google was incorporated. The name was a misspelling of 'googol,' chosen because the domain was already taken.
A neutron star packs more mass than the Sun into a sphere the size of a city. A teaspoon of its material would weigh about a billion tons on Earth.
Your body replaces roughly 3.8 million cells every second, yet the process is so orderly that your identity — down to your fingerprints — remains intact across decades.
Light from the Sun takes 8 minutes to reach Earth, but the photons themselves were generated in the solar core up to 100,000 years ago, trapped there by sheer density.
On this day in 1825, the world's first public steam railway opened in England. It is older than the photograph, the postage stamp, and the word 'scientist.'
Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the construction of the Great Pyramid.
On this day in 1540, the Jesuits received papal approval — a religious order now older than the fork becoming common table etiquette in Europe.
The fax machine was invented in 1843, before the American Civil War. Your grandparents may have used one in an office.
Oxford University was teaching students before the Aztec Empire existed. It predates the institution it would eventually outlast by two centuries.

Sonder (n.): the realization that each passerby has a life as vivid and complex as your own. Coined by John Koenig in The Dictionary of Obscure Sorrows, 2012. Now it travels faster than most words with centuries behind them.
Hiraeth (n.): a Welsh longing for a home that may never have existed. Untranslatable because English has no word for nostalgia laced with grief and the sense that belonging itself is lost.

On this day in 1825, the Stockton and Darlington Railway opened — and the word 'commuter' didn't yet exist. It arrived decades later from railroad season-ticket holders who 'commuted' their daily fares into a single discounted payment.

Petrichor (n.): the smell of rain on dry earth. Named in 1964 by Australian scientists Bear and Thomas, who combined the Greek petra (stone) and ichor, the fluid said to flow through the veins of the gods.

On this day in 1998, Google was incorporated — giving the verb 'to google' a lifespan measurable in years, not centuries. The Oxford English Dictionary added it as a lowercase verb in 2006, one of the fastest descents from proper noun to common tongue on record.
On this date in 2022, Ethereum completed The Merge, switching from proof-of-work to proof-of-stake and cutting the network's energy consumption by roughly 99.95% overnight.
On this date in 2021, El Salvador's Bitcoin Law had been in force for 26 days — the government had already bought 550 BTC using public funds before a single citizen opened the Chivo wallet.
Bitcoin's smallest unit, the satoshi, wasn't named by Satoshi Nakamoto. The community voted on the name in a 2010 Bitcointalk thread, and Satoshi never commented on it.
The DAO hack in 2016 didn't steal ether — it legitimately called a recursive withdrawal function the contract's own code permitted. Ethereum's hard fork was the irregular act, not the exploit.
Every Bitcoin block header is only 80 bytes. The entire proof-of-work security of a $1 trillion network is anchored to a data structure smaller than a tweet.

On this date in 2015, Shazam published the paper describing its neural audio fingerprinting system — but Shazam's core algorithm predates deep learning entirely, matching songs via combinatorial hash lookup since 2002.
Today in 2023, Microsoft confirmed Bing Chat had quietly surpassed 1 billion chat turns. The milestone arrived with no press release — the number emerged in an earnings call footnote.
GPT-4's training compute is estimated at around 2.15×10²⁵ FLOP. That is roughly 10,000 times the compute used to train GPT-2, released just four years earlier.

Transformers were not designed for language first. The 2017 'Attention Is All You Need' paper benchmarked exclusively on machine translation tasks; the architecture's dominance in vision, audio, and code came later as an accident of generalization.
AlphaFold 2 predicted structures for over 200 million proteins — essentially the entire known protein universe — yet the model's weights fit on a single consumer hard drive at under 500 GB.
